title: Do we still need public libraries?

turns.speaker: Samir
turns.text: Two branches are closing. The consultation document talks about book lending being down forty per cent.

turns.speaker: Jo
turns.text: Which measures the wrong thing, and I think deliberately. Almost nobody uses a library primarily for books any more.

turns.speaker: Harriet
turns.text: What do they use it for?

turns.speaker: Jo
turns.text: Printing a form. Filling in a benefits application. Sitting somewhere warm. Letting a child do homework where it's quiet.

turns.speaker: Samir
turns.text: Our branch runs the only free computer access for about a mile, and half the council's own services are online only now.

turns.speaker: Harriet
turns.text: So the council digitised its services and then closed the place where people go to use them.

turns.speaker: Samir
turns.text: That's more or less the shape of it, yes.

turns.speaker: Jo
turns.text: The other thing, and it's hard to put in a business case, is that it's one of the last indoor places you can be without buying something.

turns.speaker: Harriet
turns.text: I'd push back slightly. That argument could justify keeping any building open for ever.

turns.speaker: Samir
turns.text: It could. The counter is that the measured savings usually don't appear, because the demand goes somewhere more expensive.

turns.speaker: Harriet
turns.text: Meaning the GP, or the school.

turns.speaker: Jo
turns.text: Which is a different budget, so from where the decision is made it looks like a saving.

points: Two library branches face closure, justified by a forty per cent fall in book lending.
Jo argues lending is the wrong measure, since libraries are used for printing, forms, warmth and quiet study space.
Samir notes his branch provides the only free computer access locally while council services have moved online.
Harriet observes the contradiction of digitising services and closing the place people use to access them.
Jo adds that libraries are among the last indoor spaces requiring no purchase, though Harriet warns this argument could justify keeping anything open.
Samir argues projected savings often fail to appear because demand moves to costlier services in other budgets, which makes closure look like a saving locally.
